text: Azure Monitor is the platform-wide monitoring service watching essentially everything you've built so far in this course — the VMs from Chapter 3, the storage accounts from Chapter 4, the load balancer from Chapter 5. You don't turn it on resource by resource; it's part of the Azure platform itself. Azure Monitor is really an umbrella over several pieces — metrics, logs, alerts, dashboards — and this chapter works through them one at a time, starting with the simplest.

A metric is just a numerical value measured at a point in time, and platform metrics are the specific set Azure collects automatically for most resource types the moment they exist — no agent to install, no setting to flip on. A VM immediately starts reporting Percentage CPU, Network In and Out, and Disk Read and Write Bytes. A storage account reports transaction counts and latency the same way, with no configuration required on your part at all. That data is retained 93 days by default, which is why metrics are the first place to look when something seems off.

Metrics Explorer, in the portal, is where you chart that data over time. Four choices shape what you see: the scope, which resource or resources you're looking at; the metric itself, like Percentage CPU; the aggregation, Average, Minimum, Maximum, Sum, or Count; and the time range. Aggregation matters more than it sounds — the exact same CPU data can look perfectly calm as an Average and alarming as a Maximum, because an average quietly smooths out short, sharp spikes an administrator actually needs to see.

Say a VM feels slow. Open its Overview page, find the Percentage CPU chart, and switch the aggregation to Maximum over the last 24 hours. Pegged near 100% for long stretches is concrete evidence the VM size chosen back in Chapter 3 is too small for its real workload, not a guess. The same data is reachable from the command line too: az monitor metrics list --resource <vm-resource-id> --metric "Percentage CPU" --interval PT1H, useful once you're scripting a health check instead of clicking through the portal by hand.

Metrics tell you what's happening right now, in numbers, automatically, with no setup. But they don't tell you who did what, or capture the detailed records you'd need to investigate a real incident. Next up: Log Analytics and the Activity Log — where those detailed, queryable records actually live, including exactly who changed, created, or deleted a resource, and precisely when.
